html:
The Lex Oppia was a Roman law passed in 215 BCE, in the crisis after the Battle of Cannae, that limited how much wealth women could show. It was repealed in 195 BCE after women protested in the streets.

Proposed by the tribune Marcus Oppius, it said that no woman could own more than half an ounce of gold, wear clothes dyed in many colours, or ride in a carriage in Rome or nearby towns except for religious festivals. It was the first of Rome's sumptuary laws, laws against display, and it suited a city at war that needed every coin, during the Second Punic War.

Twenty years later the war was won and Rome was growing rich, but the law was still in force. When two tribunes proposed to repeal it, women filled the streets and the Forum and lobbied the men on their way in. The consul Cato the Elder argued against repeal, warning that women would soon want to rule; another speaker, Lucius Valerius, argued for it. The law was repealed. Livy wrote both speeches, and they are a rare look at women acting together in Roman politics.
sum: The Lex Oppia was a Roman law passed in 215 BCE, in the crisis after the Battle of Cannae, that limited how much wealth women could show. It was repealed in 195 BCE after women protested in the streets.
